title: The Opportunities and Risks AI Presents for the Economy and Financial System
summary: Governor Lisa Cook favoured holding rates steady on 27 May while judging the risks to be tilted towards higher inflation. Her baseline combined renewed disinflation, stable employment and robust near- to medium-term growth. A delay in disinflation would make her prepared to raise rates. A deterioration in employment could move her towards an easing. AI figured on both sides of that assessment. Building the infrastructure creates demand now, adding pressure to scarce inputs, while wider adoption could eventually expand productive capacity. The gains and costs need not reach prices, workers or creditors at the same time. These were Cook’s own views ahead of the release of final April PCE data (pp. 1–6).

Cook cited estimates of 3.8% headline and 3.3% core PCE inflation over the year to April. Higher gasoline prices linked to the conflict in Iran accounted for much of the headline increase. Oil futures and the forecasters she cited suggested some easing in energy prices towards year-end. Her concern was that repeated shocks could enter firms’ pricing decisions and workers’ pay negotiations before those effects faded. More than $1.5 trillion of data-centre plans had been announced, with only a small share realised. She pointed to higher prices for computing equipment and software, rising pay in specialised construction trades and increases of roughly 5% in both electricity and water prices over the past year. These figures document the scale of the proposed projects and pressure on inputs. The speech gives no estimate of how much of aggregate inflation the buildout caused (pp. 2–3, footnote 2).

Unemployment stood at 4.3% in April, little changed on balance since the preceding summer, while initial jobless claims remained low. Cook nonetheless saw downside risk from uncertainty, weak hiring and the possibility that AI-related job losses would precede new employment. She found no conclusive evidence that such displacement was already occurring. Most small firms responding to a Fed survey reported no change in labour costs from AI. Her optimism about productivity depended on firms reorganising how they produce goods and services. In finance, she described early uses in compliance, customer service and back-office systems. Better access to credit and more efficient capital allocation were potential gains whose value would depend on adoption (pp. 3–7).

For credit investors, Cook distinguished borrowers threatened by AI from those borrowing to build it. Concerns about disruption to software businesses had contributed to wider spreads on speculative-grade technology bonds and to redemption pressure at perpetual business development companies exposed to software lending. Separately, large technology firms had issued investment-grade bonds to finance capital expenditure, while smaller data-centre developers were drawing on private debt funds and asset-backed markets. Strong borrowers can still increase financial vulnerability if an investment boom becomes heavily debt-financed. Cook saw that as a risk that could build over time. Even under ambitious investment and issuance assumptions, she judged a return to pre-global-financial-crisis peak leverage unlikely (pp. 8–9).

Cook also identified risks from correlated trading, reliance on models and cyber disruption, alongside scope for stronger defences. A stylised experiment cited in the speech found less herding by AI agents than among human participants, an interesting qualification to the concern about crowded trades. The evidence came from a laboratory setting. At the Fed, staff were exploring network analysis, processing of regulatory text and scenario assessment, with verification and human review built into the work. Cook distinguished those experiments from FOMC policymaking. Her argument offers several channels through which AI could affect rates and credit, but no target for spreads or policy rates and no recommendation to buy or sell a particular exposure (pp. 8–13).

questions.question: How quickly will announced data-centre projects turn into actual spending and usable capacity?
questions.detail: Cook identifies a large pipeline and input-price pressure while leaving the conversion rate and timing uncertain. A buildout that raises demand years before capacity becomes productive would have different implications for inflation and rates from one delayed by funding or infrastructure constraints. Start with the project-level investment study and dataset cited in footnote 2. Compare announcements with construction milestones, in-service dates and realised capital spending in company filings available at the time.

questions.question: Where would a shortfall in AI-related cash flow first create a refinancing problem?
questions.detail: The speech distinguishes large investment-grade issuers from smaller developers financed privately or through asset-backed markets. It does not establish who bears utilisation risk, when debt matures, or how collateral would perform under stress. Those distinctions determine whether weaker demand first hits equities, credit spreads or lender liquidity. Examine issuer filings, collateral schedules and debt maturity disclosures alongside the May Financial Stability Report cited in footnote 6.

questions.question: What evidence would distinguish AI-related job displacement from a general slowdown in hiring?
questions.detail: Cook describes a stable aggregate labour market, weak hiring and a possible timing mismatch between job losses and gains. She finds the evidence on displacement inconclusive. The distinction matters for whether weak employment would coexist with a positive productivity outlook. Compare hiring, separations, hours and productivity by occupation and industry with contemporaneous measures of adoption. Use the Small Business Credit Survey cited in footnote 3 to check how smaller employers describe their own labour costs.
